491.title: Though the fig tree (Habakkuk 3:17–19)
491.hook: no fruit, no flock, and yet I will rejoice
491.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Habakkuk 3:17–18 in times of loss, and its words have been set in hymns and songs; Habakkuk 2:4, on the just living by faith, is quoted in Romans, Galatians and Hebrews.

segments.voice: Yesterday, little Bethlehem, the hillside village Micah pointed to. Your line was the least of the towns. Who was the overlooked person you thanked? Day four hundred ninety-one.

A prophet's usual job is to speak to the people for God. Habakkuk does something else. Habakkuk talks back to God. His book opens with a complaint, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Violence everywhere, he says, the law ignored, the wicked winning. And God's answer makes it worse: the Babylonians are coming, a fierce army that will sweep through like the desert wind. So Habakkuk climbs a watchtower, in his words, to wait and see what God will say next. Three short chapters later, he comes down singing. Today is the song.

The song ends with Habakkuk imagining the worst. In the King James: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls." Count it. Figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, cattle. For a farming people, that's everything. The pantry, the bank account, the retirement plan. All of it gone. And then one small word: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Yet. Habakkuk doesn't say things will turn out fine. He doesn't say the fig tree will bloom after all. He says even if it doesn't. His joy is anchored somewhere the harvest can't reach. Then the last picture: "he will make my feet like hinds' feet." A hind is a female deer, and in those hills deer pick their way up steep, rocky slopes without falling. The ground doesn't get easier. The feet get surer. And the book ends with a note for the choir leader, about stringed instruments, which means this cry of faith from the edge of disaster was meant to be sung together. Some Christians turn to these verses in hard seasons, and some read Habakkuk as a pattern for honest prayer: complain first, wait on the watchtower, then sing. The yet doesn't cancel the complaint. It comes after it.
screen: `NOT IF IT BLOOMS. EVEN IF IT DOESN'T.`
`FEET LIKE A DEER'S ON THE ROCKS.`
then, large: `YET I WILL REJOICE IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice in one thing on a bad day. Settle, and breathe. If today is hard, let it be hard. Name what's not blooming: money, health, a relationship, plans that fell apart. Say it plainly, the way Habakkuk listed his empty fields. Don't rush past it. Then look for one thing, just one, that's still good: a person who loves you, a breath that comes easily, light through a window, a song you know by heart. Rest your attention there. If you pray, you can say Habakkuk's yet in your own heart. If you don't, simply let that one good thing be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Though the fig tree. Habakkuk's song from the edge of disaster: even if every harvest fails, yet I will rejoice.
Your line: yet I will rejoice. Today, when something fails or falls through, finish the sentence out loud: and yet. Then name one good thing. Day four hundred ninety-one.

492.title: He will sing over you (Zephaniah 3:17)
492.hook: God will rejoice over you with singing
492.howItsDone: Some churches read Zephaniah 3:14–20 during Advent, and some Christians choose verse 17 for baptisms, weddings and blessings over children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, though the fig tree fails, Habakkuk's song from the edge. Your line was yet I will rejoice. Did you manage an and yet when something fell through? Day four hundred ninety-two.

A parent at bedtime, the same song every night, slightly off key. A whole restaurant singing happy birthday while the guest of honor tries to hide under the table. A choir at a funeral. Being sung to is strange and tender. The one being sung to does nothing at all; they just receive it. In church, the singing mostly goes one way: people sing to God. Hymns, praise songs, chants. But tucked at the end of a short book full of warnings, the direction flips. There, it's God who sings.

The book is Zephaniah, three short chapters set in the days of King Josiah. Most of it is thunder. Zephaniah warns of the day of the LORD, a day of wrath, darkness and alarm. In fact, a medieval Latin hymn about the last judgment, the Dies Irae, day of wrath, takes its opening words from Zephaniah's first chapter. So you'd expect the book to end in smoke. Instead, chapter three turns. Sing, daughter of Zion, it says. Shout. Be glad. The judgment is lifted. And then this verse, in the King James Bible: "The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing." Look at the picture. God isn't far off on a throne. God is in the midst of thee, in the middle of the crowd. God rejoices over the people like a parent over a newborn, or a groom at a wedding. And the middle phrase is a puzzle. He will rest in his love. The Hebrew can also be read as he will be silent in his love, or he will quiet you with his love. Translators read it differently. Maybe it's both: a love so deep it goes quiet, and then breaks into song. Some Christians choose this verse for baptisms and weddings, and some families paint it on a nursery wall. The God of the day of wrath, the book says, is also the God who sings over you.
screen: then, large: `HE WILL JOY OVER THEE WITH SINGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum a song over someone you love. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love: a child, a partner, a friend, a parent, maybe someone far away or someone gone. Picture them resting, safe. Then, very quietly, hum. Any tune. A lullaby, a hymn, a song from the car radio. You don't need words, and you don't need to sing well. Just let it be a song over them. Notice how it feels to rejoice over someone without asking anything back. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you hum. If you don't, simply let the song carry your care. The bell holds the time.
He will sing over you. Zephaniah's picture of God in the middle of the people, rejoicing over them with singing, after a book full of thunder.
screen: `HE WILL SING OVER YOU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sung over. Today, let someone know you're glad they exist. Out loud, in a text, or, if you're brave, in a song. Day four hundred ninety-two.

493.title: Consider your ways (Haggai 1:2–8)
493.hook: you eat but aren't full; you earn wages into a bag with holes
493.howItsDone: Some churches read Haggai when they are building or rebuilding, and some Christians use its call to consider your ways as a prompt for an honest review of how they spend their time and money.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zephaniah's surprise: he will sing over you. Your line was sung over. Did you tell someone, in words or a tune, that you're glad they exist? Day four hundred ninety-three.

Payday. The money lands in your account, and by the end of the week, somehow, it's gone. Not on anything big. Just leaking. Groceries that didn't last, subscriptions you forgot, little fixes on things that keep breaking. Working hard and never quite getting ahead. An old prophet named Haggai described exactly that, with an image anyone who's ever carried coins can picture: a bag with holes in it. He wasn't talking to people who were lazy. He was talking to people who were busy, and tired, and couldn't figure out why it never felt like enough.

Haggai's words come with dates. His first message is dated to the day: the second year of King Darius, the sixth month, the first day. The exiles have come home from Babylon to Jerusalem, and the temple is still a ruin. People are saying it isn't the right time to rebuild. Haggai's answer, in the King James Bible: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" Cieled means paneled, finished nicely, while God's house sits in rubble. Then comes the line that becomes today's carry: "Consider your ways." In Hebrew it's more vivid: set your heart on your ways. Look hard at where your life is going. And then the list: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes." Every line has the same shape. Effort in, nothing to show for it. Haggai's diagnosis is that the people have put their own houses first and left the center empty. So the cure is surprisingly practical: go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build. Christians read Haggai in more than one way. Some hear it about church buildings and giving. Others hear it more broadly: when the most important thing in a life is left in ruins, everything else leaks. And then the people listened. Before the month was out, by Haggai's own dates, they started rebuilding.
screen: `DATED TO THE DAY: A TEMPLE IN RUINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at where your effort leaks. Settle, and breathe. Picture your last week as a bag you've been filling. Your time, your energy, your money, your attention. Where are the holes? Maybe it's hours on a screen that left you emptier. Maybe it's worry about something you can't change. Maybe it's work that never touches what you care most about. Don't fix it now. Just find one hole. Then ask Haggai's question: what's the thing at the center that I've left in ruins? If you pray, you can set that before God and ask for one first step. If you don't, simply name it, and name the first piece of wood. The bell holds the time.
Consider your ways. Haggai's call to returned exiles who were busy and never satisfied: set your heart on where your life is going.
Your line: consider your ways. Today, patch one hole in the bag. Close one tab, cancel one thing, or give ten minutes to what matters most. Day four hundred ninety-three.

494.title: Not by might (Zechariah 4:6)
494.hook: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit
494.tomorrow: your king comes on a donkey
494.howItsDone: Some Christians quote Zechariah 4:6 when starting a work that feels too big, such as founding a church or a ministry, and some read the lampstand's oil as a picture of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Haggai and the bag with holes. Your line was consider your ways. Which hole did you patch, and what did you give ten minutes to? Day four hundred ninety-four.

Same city, same year, same half-built temple as yesterday. Haggai had told the people to get building, and they did. The man in charge of the job is Zerubbabel, the governor, a descendant of the old kings, working with a small crew of returned exiles, not much money, hostile neighbors, and a foundation that looks like nothing next to the stories of Solomon's temple. Haggai himself asks who is left who saw the first house in its glory, and whether this one looks like nothing beside it. Into that discouragement steps a second prophet named Zechariah. And he doesn't bring a budget. He brings a vision.

In the vision, Zechariah sees a lampstand of solid gold with seven lamps, and on either side, two olive trees. The trees seem to feed oil straight into the lamps. Nobody has to press olives, haul jars or refill anything. The light just keeps burning, fed from a source the lamps don't control. Zechariah asks the angel what it means, and the answer, in the King James Bible, is this: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts." The word for might can also mean an army, or wealth, or strength. Power is the strength of your own arm. Zerubbabel has neither. And God says, that's fine. That's not how this gets built. Then a picture for the governor's problem: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain." The mountain might be the opposition, or the sheer size of the task. Either way, it flattens. And when the last stone goes on, the people will shout grace, grace unto it. A few verses later comes a question that's worth putting on a sticky note: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" The little foundation that looked like nothing is not to be despised. Small beginnings count. Some Christians read Zechariah's vision as a picture of the Holy Spirit, the oil that keeps the lamp burning. Others hear it as a word for any work that seems too big for the people doing it: churches, families, movements, or one person trying to change. The work still needs hands. Zerubbabel still lays the stones. But the light isn't his to manufacture.
screen: `OIL FROM A SOURCE BEYOND THE LAMP.`
then, large: `NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER, BUT BY MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of forcing one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been pushing on hard: a person you're trying to change, a project that won't move, an outcome you're gripping with both hands. Notice the clench, in your jaw, your shoulders, your stomach. Now, for a few breaths, loosen it. You're not quitting. Zerubbabel kept building. You're just admitting that the oil isn't yours to make. Picture the two olive trees feeding the lamp, quietly, without effort. If you pray, you can hand that one thing to God's spirit. If you don't, simply let your hands open on your lap. The bell holds the time.
Not by might. Zechariah's word to a governor with a small crew and a big job: not by army, not by strength, but by God's spirit.
Your line: not by might. Today, when you catch yourself forcing, step back once. Do your part, and leave the rest unforced. Day four hundred ninety-four.

495.title: Your king comes on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9)
495.hook: lowly and riding on a donkey: words the gospels saw on Palm Sunday
495.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday, the Sunday before Easter, many churches hold processions with palm branches and read the Gospel of Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey, often alongside Zechariah 9:9.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah's lampstand and the word to Zerubbabel: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit. Did you manage to stop forcing one thing? Day four hundred ninety-five.

Leaders arrive with motorcades and flashing lights, or a jet on the tarmac. In the ancient world, a conquering king rode in on a warhorse, or stood in a chariot, with soldiers marching behind and captives in chains. The animal said everything: I won, and I can do it again. A different arrival: crowds, shouting, branches in the road, and at the center of it, a man on a young donkey, his feet nearly scraping the ground. Many churches remember that scene every year on Palm Sunday. But the picture was painted centuries earlier, in the same book as yesterday's vision.

Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass." Ass is the old English word for a donkey. And notice what Zechariah does. He announces a king, the trumpets are ready, and then he says lowly. The Hebrew word can also mean poor, or humbled. A king who is just and brings rescue, but comes without swagger. The next verse explains why the donkey matters. God says the chariot and the warhorse will be cut off, the battle bow broken, and this king will speak peace to the nations. A donkey is the animal of farmers and traders, of ordinary days. It's a peace animal. The king arrives disarmed on purpose. Centuries later, the Gospels tell how Jesus sent two disciples to bring a donkey and rode it down the Mount of Olives into Jerusalem, as the crowds spread cloaks and branches. Matthew and John both quote Zechariah to explain it. And here's a curious detail. Zechariah, like much Hebrew poetry, says the same thing twice: an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass. Matthew's account has two animals, a donkey and her colt. Readers have discussed that for centuries. Jews still read Zechariah's king as a hope for the future, and Christians hear it as fulfilled on Palm Sunday. Either way the picture holds: power that chooses to come low.
screen: then, large: `LOWLY, AND RIDING UPON AN ASS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice humble strength. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you have some power: as a parent, a boss, an older sibling, the person who knows the most in the room, the one with the car keys. Notice how you usually use it. On a warhorse, or on a donkey? Now picture one situation coming up where you could choose the donkey. Ask instead of order. Listen before deciding. Let someone else go first. Lowly doesn't mean weak; the king in Zechariah is still a king. If you pray, you can ask for that kind of strength. If you don't, simply picture yourself arriving gently. The bell holds the time.
Ani, Hebrew for lowly, poor or humbled: Zechariah's word for a just king arriving lowly, on the animal of peace, which the Gospels saw on Palm Sunday.
Your line: lowly, riding. Today, in one place where you hold the power, arrive on the donkey. Ask, listen, or go last. Day four hundred ninety-five.

496.title: Turn the hearts (Malachi 4:5–6)
496.hook: the last lines of the Protestant Old Testament: hearts of parents turned to children
496.howItsDone: Some churches read Malachi in Advent, as the prophecy of a messenger before the Lord, and pair it with the Gospel stories of John the Baptist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your king comes on a donkey, lowly and riding, with no warhorse. Your line was lowly, riding. Where did you choose the donkey instead of the horse? Day four hundred ninety-six.

In a Protestant Bible, the Old Testament ends with Malachi. Turn the page, and the next thing is the first line of Matthew, a list of names. Between them sits a silence the Bible doesn't fill. So whatever Malachi says last stands right at the seam. You might expect a grand vision, or a thunderclap. Instead, the final words are about something very small and very close to home. They're about families. Parents and children. Who's speaking to whom, and who isn't.

Malachi's name means my messenger, and it may be a title rather than a name. His book is a series of arguments between God and the people, about tired worship, broken promises and marriages, and the poor being cheated. Then the end, in the King James Bible: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Elijah, remember, doesn't die in 2 Kings. He's carried up in a whirlwind. So the hope grew that he'd come back, to prepare the way for God. At the Passover seder, Jewish tradition pours a cup for Elijah and opens the door for him. And look at what Elijah's work will be. Not to defeat enemies. To mend families. To turn hearts across the generations, in both directions. Parents toward children, and children toward parents. Then the very last words warn that otherwise God will strike the land with a curse. That ending is so hard that in synagogue readings the verse before it is read again afterward, so the book closes on Elijah and hope. You'll hear these words again very soon. In the opening chapter of Luke, an angel promises that a child named John will come in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. Christians read John the Baptist as the Elijah Malachi promised. So the Old Testament, in this arrangement, ends with a family reunion still waiting to happen.
screen: then, large: `HE SHALL TURN THE HEART OF THE FATHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call a parent or child. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone a generation away from you: a parent or a child, or if they're gone or far away, a grandparent, a niece, a mentor, someone you've cared for. Picture their face. Notice what's between you: warmth, distance, an old hurt, a thing unsaid. Don't try to fix it all. Just let your heart turn toward them, a few degrees, the way Malachi pictures it. Then decide on one small contact: a call, a message, a photo, a visit. If you pray, you can bring them before God by name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Malachi, meaning my messenger: his last promise that Elijah would come and turn the hearts of parents to children, and children to parents.
Your line: open the door for Elijah. Today, make the call or send the message you chose. Ask one question and actually listen to the answer. Day four hundred ninety-six.

497.title: Wipe away tears (Isaiah 25:6–8)
497.hook: a feast of rich food for all peoples, and death swallowed up
497.howItsDone: Isaiah 25:6–9 is among the funeral readings in some churches, and some Christians connect its feast with the communion meal and with the hope of resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi's last promise, Elijah sent to turn the hearts of parents and children. Your line was open the door for Elijah. Did you make the call or send the message? Day four hundred ninety-seven.

After a funeral, there's usually food. A long table in a church hall, casseroles under foil, someone's famous potato salad, coffee in big urns. People who haven't seen each other in years stand around holding paper plates, and between the tears there's sometimes laughter. Grief and a meal, side by side. Today the book of Isaiah takes that same table and turns it inside out: a feast where the guest list is everyone on earth. And the main thing that's been swallowed up, at the end of the meal, is death.
screen: `GRIEF AND A MEAL, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the menu, in the King James Bible: "a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined." Fat things meant the best food, the richest cuts. Wine on the lees is wine left to age on its sediment until it's deep and smooth. This isn't a snack. It's a banquet, set on God's mountain, and it's for all people, every nation. Then the feast takes a turn. God removes the covering cast over all peoples, the veil spread over all nations. Some readers hear that as a burial shroud, the cloth laid over the dead, and it's lifted off the whole human race. And then this: "He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Some readers hear an echo of older stories from that region, where death was a swallower with a huge mouth. Here, the swallower gets swallowed. And then a gentle picture. After the victory, God doesn't make a speech. God goes face to face, wiping tears off cheeks, one by one, like a parent after a nightmare. The New Testament picks these words up twice. Paul quotes the swallowing of death when he writes about the resurrection. And near the very end of the Bible, Revelation says: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Christians hear in this feast a picture of what they hope for. This week's prophets have walked us there: Habakkuk's yet, the God who sings, consider your ways, not by might, the donkey king, hearts turned. And now, a table set for everyone.
